reference_title: Ground Modification Methods Reference Manual – Volume I

sections.title: Description and History
sections.summary: Introduces column-supported embankments (CSE) as a ground modification approach for building highway embankments over soft compressible soils when time constraints are critical, with or without a geosynthetic reinforced load transfer platform (LTP).
sections.body: Constructing highway embankments over soft compressible soils brings large settlements, embankment instability and long consolidation times, problems that led to many ground modification techniques: prefabricated vertical drains (PVDs), surcharge loading, geosynthetic reinforcement, stone columns, deep soil mixing and lightweight fill. When time constraints are critical to the success of a project, owners have resorted to column supported embankments (CSE), with or without a geosynthetic reinforced load transfer platform (LTP). The manual notes that in the last 25 years the technology has been used successfully by over a dozen state DOTs (p. 6-1).
key_points: CSE is used where time constraints rule out waiting for consolidation of soft foundation soil.
A CSE may be built with or without a geosynthetic reinforced load transfer platform (LTP).
sections.applicability: Introduction to CSE technology for embankments over soft compressible soils.

sections.title: Description
sections.summary: Container heading for the description of a column-supported embankment system: the embankment on stiff columns, the support column types that may be used, and the load transfer platform that carries load onto the columns.
sections.body: This heading groups the description of the three parts of the system: the column-supported embankment itself (6.1.1.1), the support columns (6.1.1.2) and the load transfer platform (6.1.1.3), pp. 6-1 to 6-3.

sections.title: Column-supported Embankments
sections.summary: CSEs are stiff vertical columns that carry embankment load through soft soil to a firm foundation; columns close enough together allow soil arching so the full load reaches the columns. Columns are typically 4 to 6 ft apart, and an LTP reduces the number of columns needed.
sections.body: CSEs consist of stiff vertical columns designed to transfer the load of the embankment through the soft compressible soil layer to a firm foundation. The column type depends on design loads, constructability and cost. The embankment load must be effectively transferred to the columns to prevent punching of the columns through the embankment fill, which causes differential settlement at the embankment surface. If the columns are placed close enough together, soil arching will occur and the full embankment load will be transferred to the columns (Figure 6-1, p. 6-1). The columns in Figure 6-1 are spaced relatively close together (4 to 6 feet), and some battered columns may be required at the sides of the embankment to prevent lateral spreading. To significantly reduce the number of columns and increase the efficiency of the design, a load transfer platform (LTP), either geosynthetically reinforced or unreinforced, may be used (Figure 6-2, p. 6-2). Figure 6-2 defines the profile: general embankment fill over select fill and geosynthetic reinforcement, H = H1 + H2, surcharge q, side slope n:1, upper sand layer(s) if present, soft soil layer(s), bearing layer and dw.
key_points: Columns spaced close enough together allow soil arching so the full embankment load is carried by the columns.
Without an LTP columns are relatively close (4 to 6 ft); battered columns may be needed at the sides against lateral spreading.
An LTP, reinforced or unreinforced, reduces the number of columns required.

sections.title: Support Columns
sections.summary: Lists the column types used in CSEs: steel H-piles, steel pipe piles, auger cast piles, precast concrete and timber piles, plus formed-in-place soil mix, aggregate and cement based columns; the technology is not tied to any one column type.
sections.body: Support columns used with this technology include steel H-piles, steel pipe piles, auger cast piles, precast concrete piles and timber piles. Conventional steel and concrete piles often provide higher axial capacity than a CSE requires and are therefore less economically attractive than timber piles and the newer formed-in-place column types: soil mix columns, aggregate columns and cement based columns (covered in Chapter 7 Soil Mixing and Chapter 5 Aggregate Columns). Column selection depends on the design loads, the foundation support layer, any stiff intermediate layers that must be penetrated, special equipment requirements, speed of installation, and local availability and cost. The technology is not dependent on any one column type, which lets the contractor select the most economical column for the design and performance requirements set by the specifying agency (pp. 6-2 to 6-3).
key_points: Conventional steel and concrete piles often exceed the capacity a CSE needs and are less economical than timber piles and formed-in-place columns.
The technology is not dependent on any one column type; the contractor may pick the most economical column meeting the requirements.
sections.applicability: Choosing among column types for a column-supported embankment.

sections.title: Load Transfer Platform
sections.summary: The LTP transfers embankment load to the columns without deformation between columns reflecting to the surface. Three types exist: a reinforced concrete mat (generally cost prohibitive), and granular fill with or without geosynthetic. Reinforced LTPs follow either the catenary or the beam method.
sections.body: The load transfer platform (LTP) efficiently transfers the embankment or structure load to the columns without allowing unacceptable deformations between columns that would reflect to the embankment surface. Three types are available. A reinforced concrete structural mat requires structural design; concrete mats have generally been found cost prohibitive and are not discussed further. The second and third types are select granular structural fill either reinforced with one or more layers of geosynthetic, or unreinforced; the chapter focuses on granular LTPs. There are two fundamental approaches to geosynthetic reinforced LTPs. The catenary method considers the reinforcement to act as one layer at the interface between the subgrade and columns and the embankment, acting as a catenary; select fill may or may not be used above it. The beam method considers multiple (3 or more) layers of reinforcement spaced vertically, typically 8 to 16 inches apart, within the LTP to create a beam of reinforced soil (p. 6-3).
key_points: Concrete structural mats are generally cost prohibitive and are not covered further.
Granular LTPs may be reinforced with one or more geosynthetic layers or unreinforced.
Catenary method: one reinforcement layer at the column/subgrade interface acting as a catenary.
Beam method: 3 or more layers spaced typically 8 to 16 in. apart forming a reinforced soil beam.
sections.applicability: Types of load transfer platform used with column-supported embankments.

sections.title: Historical Overview
sections.summary: History of CSE with geosynthetic reinforcement: first highway use in 1984 in Europe, first U.S. use in 1994 for a storage tank on vibro-concrete columns, early transportation use in 2001, and the shift in U.S. design practice from the beam method to the load and displacement compatibility (LDC) method.
sections.body: The first documented highway use of CSE with geosynthetic reinforcement was in 1984 for a bridge approach embankment in Europe (Reid and Buchanan 1984): concrete piles with reinforced concrete pile caps, a clear span between caps of 6.6 to 10 feet, one geosynthetic layer forming the LTP, and a 30-foot high embankment. The first U.S. application was in 1994 for a large-diameter molasses storage tank founded on vibro-concrete columns (VCC) and an LTP of well graded granular fill reinforced with three geogrid layers, chosen over a pile foundation with a concrete mat for time and cost savings (Figure 6-3). One of the first (2001) U.S. transportation projects used VCCs on a 6.6 to 10 feet center-to-center triangular spacing with a 3-foot thick LTP reinforced with three geogrid layers for an embankment at a river crossing, to eliminate the bump at the end of the bridge without waiting for consolidation (Young et al. 2003; Figure 6-4). More than 20 case histories were documented by 1999 (Han 1999). U.S. design practice first relied on the semi-empirical beam method; it is being replaced by the more analytically correct load and displacement compatibility (LDC) method (Sloan et al. 2013), and some designers use 2D and 3D numerical deformation analyses (pp. 6-3 to 6-6).
key_points: First documented highway use: 1984 bridge approach in Europe, 30 ft embankment, one geosynthetic layer, 6.6 to 10 ft clear span between caps.
First U.S. use: 1994, VCCs with a three-geogrid LTP under a storage tank.
2001 transportation use: VCCs at 6.6 to 10 ft triangular spacing, 3 ft LTP with three geogrid layers.
The semi-empirical beam method is being replaced by the LDC method (Sloan et al. 2013).

sections.title: Focus and Scope
sections.summary: States the chapter's aim: identify problems solved by CSE, synthesize the current state of practice in CSE design and construction, give selection guidance, and provide references and typical costs for preliminary technical and economic evaluation.
sections.body: The focus of the chapter is to identify problems that have been successfully solved by CSEs and to synthesize the current state of the practice of CSE construction and design. It also gives guidance on the selection process for when and where to use CSEs. References are cited for more detailed technical information, and typical costs are given so that a preliminary technical and economic evaluation can be made of whether a CSE can solve a specific problem. The document is intended to serve as a reference on CSEs, discussing their construction, utilization and limitations (p. 6-6).
sections.applicability: Defines what the CSE chapter covers.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.summary: Defines terms used in the chapter: aggregate columns, CSE, cement based columns, driven pile columns, the LDC design method, the LTP, geosynthetics, PVDs, reinforcement and vibro-concrete columns (VCC).
sections.body: Definitions given on pp. 6-6 to 6-7: Aggregate columns are stone columns and rammed aggregate piers capable of supporting 25 to 150 kips of vertical load. A Column Supported Embankment (CSE) consists of stiff vertical columns designed to transfer embankment load through the soft compressible layer to a firm foundation. Cement based columns use Portland cement binder with aggregate and are more rigid than aggregate columns; concrete options include vibro-concrete columns (VCCs), controlled modulus columns (CMCs) and continuous flight auger (CFA) piles. Driven pile columns are conventional piles (steel H, steel pipe, timber) used to support an embankment. Load and Displacement Compatibility (LDC) is the CSE design methodology recommended in the chapter. The Load Transfer Platform (LTP) is select granular structural fill, reinforced with one or more geosynthetic layers or unreinforced, that transfers load to the columns without unacceptable deformation reflecting to the surface. Geosynthetics include geogrids, geotextiles and geostraps. A Prefabricated Vertical Drain (PVD) is a band-shaped product with a geotextile jacket around a plastic core. Reinforcement refers to inclusions with continuous soil-inclusion stress transfer. Vibro-Concrete Columns (VCC) are related to stone columns, with concrete replacing the stone.
key_points: Aggregate columns: 25 to 150 kips vertical load.
LDC is the CSE design methodology recommended in the chapter.

sections.title: Primary References

sections.body: The primary references for the chapter (pp. 6-7 to 6-8) are: Collin (2007), on the U.S. state of practice for design of the geosynthetic reinforced LTP in CSEs (ASCE GSP 172); Filz and Smith (2007), on net vertical loads on geosynthetic reinforcement in CSEs (GSP 172); Filz, McGuire, Sloan, Collin and Smith (2012), on CSE settlement and load transfer (GeoCongress 2012 keynote, GSP 226); and Sloan, Filz and Collin (2013), on CSE field tests and design recommendations (Center for Geotechnical Practice, Virginia Tech).

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Introduces the section on CSE feasibility: applications, advantages and disadvantages, feasibility evaluations (geotechnical, environmental, site), limitations and alternative improvement methods.
sections.body: This section discusses applications, advantages and disadvantages, feasibility evaluations, limitations, and alternative solutions for the CSE technology (p. 6-9).
sections.applicability: Overview of how to judge whether a CSE suits a project.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: CSEs support embankments over soft soil when there is no time for consolidation with PVDs and surcharge, or when settlement and stability govern. Transportation uses include embankment stabilization, roadway widening, bridge approach fills, and bridge abutment and other foundation support, including MSE walls on CSEs.
sections.body: CSEs have traditionally supported embankments over soft soil when time is not available for consolidation using PVDs and surcharge, or when differential or total settlement and overall stability are a concern. The main purpose is to transfer embankment load through the columns to a competent soil or rock layer below the soft soil. Transportation applications include embankment stabilization, roadway widening, bridge approach fill stabilization, and bridge abutment and other foundation support; other uses include storage tanks, building foundations and retaining wall support. For large area loads, CSE is a practical alternative where conventional embankments cannot be built due to stability, time or environmental considerations, including moderate to high fills and fills contained by MSE walls. For widening next to existing highways on soft soils, CSE mitigates differential settlement between existing and new construction. For bridge approaches CSE provides stability and reduces maintenance at the bridge joint; the manual cites a 2001 light rail approach embankment on VCCs with three geosynthetic layers (Young et al. 2003). Under favorable conditions CSEs can be built higher than a conventional approach embankment, so bridge length may be reduced, and fill can be placed quickly because little load reaches the soft soil. CSEs can support abutments, MSE walls and building foundations (pp. 6-9 to 6-10).
key_points: Used when time is not available for consolidation, or when total/differential settlement and stability are a concern.
Transportation applications: embankment stabilization, roadway widening, bridge approach fill stabilization, bridge abutment and other foundation support.
CSEs can be built higher than conventional approach embankments on soft soil, potentially shortening bridges.
MSE walls may be supported on CSEs.
sections.applicability: Identifying project types where a CSE is appropriate.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of CSE
sections.summary: Container heading for the advantages of column-supported embankments (rapid one-stage construction, flexibility of column type) and their potential disadvantages (mainly high initial cost).
sections.body: This heading groups the advantages of CSE (6.2.2.1) and its potential disadvantages (6.2.2.2), pp. 6-10 to 6-11.
sections.applicability: Weighing CSE against other embankment construction approaches.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Key advantage: construction can proceed rapidly in one stage with no waiting for pore pressure dissipation. CSEs can be cheaper than removal and replacement, can avoid vibration, greatly reduce total and differential settlement, may be more sustainable, and are not limited to one column type.
sections.body: CSEs are a technical and potentially economical alternative to surcharge loading with PVDs and to staged construction with or without geosynthetic reinforcement. The key advantage is that construction may proceed rapidly in one stage with no waiting for dissipation of pore water pressure in the soft foundation soil. CSEs are also more economical than removal and replacement of deep soft deposits, particularly on larger sites with shallow groundwater. Where infrastructure precludes high-vibration techniques, the column type can be selected to minimize or eliminate vibrations. Total and differential settlement may be drastically reduced compared with conventional approaches, and CSEs may be a sustainable alternative (e.g., less energy intensive than constructing and removing a temporary surcharge). A major benefit is that the technology is not limited to any one column type: columns with no spoils can be chosen for contaminated sites; cement based columns, auger cast-in-place piles or timber piles for very soft soil; stone columns or rammed aggregate piers may be more attractive in stronger soils (pp. 6-10 to 6-11).
key_points: Construction may proceed rapidly in one stage with no waiting for pore pressure dissipation.
Often more economical than removal and replacement of deep soft soils.
Column type can be chosen to limit vibration or to avoid spoils on contaminated sites.
sections.applicability: Advantages of CSE compared with conventional soft-ground embankment methods.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: The major disadvantage of CSE is often a high initial construction cost, though including time savings and reduced long-term maintenance in the economic analysis may make it far less costly than other solutions.
sections.body: A major disadvantage of CSE is often its high initial construction cost compared with other solutions. However, if the time savings and the reduced maintenance from improved long-term performance are included in the economic analysis, the cost may be far less than that of other solutions (p. 6-11).
key_points: High initial construction cost is the main disadvantage.
Time savings and reduced maintenance should be included in the economic comparison.
sections.applicability: Economic drawbacks to weigh when considering a CSE.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: General feasibility criteria for CSE: embankment heights to date under about 50 ft; area replacement ratio typically 3.5 to 10% (as low as 2.5%); height above critical height; LTP fill friction angle at least 35 degrees; columns carry the whole load; clear span 10 ft or less; post-construction settlement typically under 2 to 4 in.
sections.body: CSE may be used whenever an embankment must be built on soft compressible soil; to date the technology has been limited to embankment heights less than about 50 feet. The depth of the soft layer is typically not critical because many column types can reach a firm layer below it. Factors to consider (pp. 6-11 to 6-12): (1) preliminary column spacing has typically been limited so that the area replacement ratio is between 3.5 and 10%, on some projects as low as 2.5%; the area replacement ratio is the plan area of the column (or of the column cap, if caps are used) divided by the plan area of the unit cell, the area of influence of each column; this is based on the empirical performance of documented case histories (see Section 4.2). (2) The embankment height should be greater than the critical height, the minimum height at which there is no practically significant differential settlement at the embankment surface; column or cap width and spacing strongly influence it (see Section 4.5). (3) LTP fill shall be a select structural fill with an effective friction angle of 35 degrees or more. (4) Columns shall be designed to carry the entire embankment load. (5) The clear span between columns should be 10 feet or less. (6) CSE typically reduces post-construction settlement of the embankment surface to less than 2 to 4 inches and differential settlement to less than 1 inch.
key_points: Embankment heights to date less than about 50 ft.
Area replacement ratio typically 3.5 to 10%, as low as 2.5%; use cap area when column caps are used.
Embankment height should exceed the critical height.
LTP select fill effective friction angle >= 35 degrees.
Columns designed to carry the entire embankment load.
Clear span between columns <= 10 ft.
Post-construction settlement typically < 2 to 4 in.; differential settlement < 1 in.
sections.applicability: Preliminary screening of CSE feasibility and column spacing.

sections.title: Geotechnical Considerations
sections.summary: Key geotechnical questions for CSE feasibility: whether soft soil extends to grade (needing a working platform), whether surface soils can act as or assist the LTP, and whether stiff intermediate strata block column penetration. These affect economy but are not deal breakers.
sections.body: The key geotechnical considerations when evaluating CSE feasibility are: (1) Does the soft compressible soil extend to grade so that a working platform will be required before installing the columns? (2) If soft soils do not extend to grade, are the surface soils adequate in strength, stiffness and layer thickness to act as the LTP or to assist the LTP in distributing embankment load to the columns? (3) Are there intermediate strata of relatively stiff or dense soils that cannot be penetrated by the columns? These factors affect the overall economy of the system but are not considered deal breakers for use of the technology (p. 6-12).
key_points: A working platform may be needed if soft soil extends to grade.
Competent surface soils may act as or assist the LTP.
Impenetrable stiff intermediate strata affect economy but do not rule out CSE.
sections.applicability: Geotechnical site questions when screening a CSE.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Column selection should consider environmental effects of installation, such as fines-laden jetting water from wet vibro-replacement stone columns and possible release of contaminants, and noise and vibration in urban settings; non-replacement column systems are an alternative.
sections.body: The selection of the most appropriate column system should consider the environmental effects of installation. For example, vibro-replacement stone columns are traditionally jetted in place, removing the finer portion of the influenced soil; the fines-laden jetting water must be temporarily contained for sediment deposition and disposal, regulations vary by jurisdiction, and unknown contaminants may be removed and transferred to the environment by the jetting water. The designer may select an alternate column system that does not replace the in situ soils, such as dry vibro-displacement stone columns or cement based columns. In urban environments where noise and vibration may be unacceptable, columns may be selected accordingly (p. 6-12).
key_points: Wet vibro-replacement produces fines-laden water needing containment and may mobilize contaminants.
Non-replacement systems (dry vibro-displacement, cement based columns) avoid this.
Noise and vibration may govern column choice in urban areas.
sections.applicability: Environmental factors in choosing CSE columns.

sections.title: Site Consideration
sections.summary: Few site constraints rule out CSE because column type can change with site conditions, including limited headroom; LTP thickness relative to groundwater can be a constraint, as in the printed example of a 4 ft LTP under an MSE wall leveling pad requiring excavation below the water table.
sections.body: Site conditions should always be considered when selecting a ground improvement technology. CSE may be used on sites with limited headroom because the column type can be changed to suit the site, and there are not many site constraints the technology cannot accommodate. An important consideration is the thickness of the LTP. For example, if an MSE wall is to be placed on the LTP, the MSE leveling pad is 2 feet below existing grade and the water table is 3 feet below existing grade, a 4-foot thick LTP would be difficult to construct because it would require 3 feet of excavation below the groundwater table (pp. 6-12 to 6-13).
key_points: Column type can be changed for limited headroom and other site constraints.
LTP thickness relative to the groundwater table can make construction difficult.
sections.applicability: Site constraints affecting CSE and LTP construction.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: The major limitation of CSE is for very low embankments on soft soils starting at the ground surface, where columns may have to be so close to satisfy the critical height requirement that the system becomes uneconomical.
sections.body: The major limitation of this technology is that for very low height embankments on soft soil projects where the soft soils start at the ground surface, the columns may need to be so close together to satisfy the critical height design requirement that the CSE system becomes uneconomical (p. 6-13).
key_points: Very low embankments on soft soil starting at grade may need uneconomically close column spacing to meet the critical height.
sections.applicability: When a CSE may not be economical.

sections.title: Alternative Improvement Methods
sections.summary: Alternatives to consider when evaluating CSE: surcharge preloading with or without PVDs, staged construction with or without geosynthetic reinforcement, lightweight fill, combinations of these, and a bridge structure instead of an embankment over soft soil.
sections.body: Alternate ground improvement systems to consider when evaluating CSE include surcharge pre-loading with or without PVDs, staged construction with or without geosynthetic reinforcement, lightweight fill, and combinations of these technologies. The chapters on Vertical Drains and Accelerated Consolidation, Lightweight Fills and Reinforced Soil Structures should be reviewed for these systems. Designers should also consider a bridge structure as an alternative to an embankment when crossing soft compressible soil sites (p. 6-13).
key_points: Alternatives: surcharge with or without PVDs, staged construction, lightweight fill, combinations, or a bridge structure.
sections.applicability: Comparing CSE with other soft-ground solutions.

sections.title: Materials and Construction
sections.summary: Introduces the materials and construction of the two main CSE components: the columns (materials, construction, column caps) and the load transfer platforms (granular material, geosynthetic reinforcement, construction).
sections.body: This section covers the materials and construction of CSE columns (Section 3.1: materials, construction and column caps) and of load transfer platforms (Section 3.2: granular material, geosynthetic reinforcement and construction), pp. 6-14 to 6-18.
sections.applicability: Materials and construction practice for CSE columns and LTPs.

sections.title: Columns
sections.summary: Container heading for CSE columns: the column materials and types with their capacities (Table 6-1), column construction and working platforms, and column caps used to reduce the clear span.
sections.body: This heading groups the column materials (6.3.1.1), column construction (6.3.1.2) and column caps (6.3.1.3), pp. 6-14 to 6-16.
sections.applicability: CSE column materials and installation.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Column options for CSE: driven piles (modulus 1,000 to 30,000 ksi; timber 1,000 ksi), CFA piles, cement based columns (often proprietary), and aggregate columns (modulus 5 to 9 ksi). Table 6-1 gives allowable capacity, typical lengths and diameters for each type.
sections.body: Many column types are available. Driven pile columns (timber, steel H, steel pipe, precast concrete, cast-in-place concrete shell, and shells driven without mandrel) are very stiff, with a modulus of elasticity between 1,000 and 30,000 ksi (1,000 ksi for timber); capacity per GEC 12 (2016). Continuous flight auger (CFA) piles use concrete and are stiff columns; capacity per GEC 8 (2007); settlement of these columns is typically governed by the capacity of the foundation soil. Other cement based columns (cemented aggregate or Portland cement concrete) are related to aggregate columns, are often proprietary, and some suit installation below the water table or in very soft soils. Aggregate columns (stone columns and rammed aggregate piers) have modulus values of 5 to 9 ksi, much lower than driven piles or cement based columns (design in Chapter 5). Table 6-1 (p. 6-15) lists allowable capacity (kips), typical lengths (ft) and diameters (in.): timber 25-100, 20-60, 12-18; steel H 100-450, 30-100, 10-14; steel pipe 175-550, 30-120, 10-48; precast concrete 100-450, 30-50, 10-24; cast-in-place shell (mandrel driven) 100-300, 20-120, 10-18; shells without mandrel 110-300, 20-75, 12-36; CFA 75-150, 20-75, 12-24; DMM 90-275, 20-90, 24-78; aggregate columns 25-150, 10-30, 24-48; VCC 50-300, 20-90, 18-24; CSV 5-10, 10-30, 5-7; CMC 50-150, 20-90, 12-24.
key_points: Driven piles: modulus 1,000 to 30,000 ksi (timber 1,000 ksi).
Aggregate columns: modulus 5 to 9 ksi.
Timber pile allowable capacity 25 to 100 kips; steel pipe 175 to 550 kips; CFA 75 to 150 kips; VCC 50 to 300 kips; CMC 50 to 150 kips (Table 6-1).
Driven pile capacity per GEC 12 (2016); CFA per GEC 8 (2007).
sections.applicability: Selecting a column type and its typical capacity for a CSE.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Column installation uses specialized, often large and heavy equipment; construction guidance is in the Aggregate Columns and Soil Mixing chapters, GEC 8 and GEC 12. A working platform may be needed on soft soils, and any geosynthetic in it is not part of the LTP analysis.
sections.body: Column installation typically involves specialized construction equipment. The chapters on Aggregate Columns and Soil Mixing cover construction techniques and equipment for aggregate, cement based and soil mix columns; CFA piles are covered in GEC 8 (2007) and driven piles in GEC 12 (2016). Most column installation equipment is relatively large and may be heavy, so on soft soil projects a working platform may be required for access. The working platform may include a layer of geosynthetic reinforcement to stabilize the subgrade; this layer is solely for the working platform and should not be included in the LTP analysis. See Chapter 9 Pavement Support Stabilization Technologies for stabilization design and construction guidance (p. 6-15).
key_points: A working platform may be required on soft sites for heavy installation equipment.
Working-platform geosynthetic should not be counted in the LTP analysis.
sections.applicability: Constructing CSE columns on soft sites.

sections.title: Column Caps
sections.summary: Column caps reduce the clear span between columns and are usually cast-in-place or precast concrete, possibly reinforced. Little design information exists; issues center on the column-to-cap connection for lateral loads and bending moments.
sections.body: Column caps are used to decrease the clear span between columns; a CSE with a geosynthetic LTP and column caps is shown in Figure 6-5. Caps usually consist of cast-in-place or precast concrete, and reinforcing steel may be required. There is currently little information on the design of column caps. Design issues focus on the connection between column and cap with respect to lateral loads and bending moments (how lateral loads are determined and where they are applied), pp. 6-15 to 6-16.
key_points: Caps decrease the clear span between columns.
Little design guidance exists; the column-cap connection under lateral load and moment is the main issue.
figures: Figure 6-5: CSE with column caps.
sections.applicability: Use and design issues of column caps in a CSE.

sections.title: Load Transfer Platforms
sections.summary: LTPs covered in the manual are select granular structural fill, unreinforced or reinforced with one or more geosynthetic layers, or in situ unreinforced cohesionless soil.
sections.body: The LTPs covered in this manual consist of select granular structural fill, either non-reinforced or reinforced with one or more layers of geosynthetic reinforcement, or in situ unreinforced cohesionless soil (p. 6-16).
sections.applicability: Types of LTP addressed in the manual.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: LTP materials: a stiff, deep enough surface soil layer may act as the LTP, otherwise well graded frictional granular fill is used; reinforcement is a single high-strength geotextile or geogrid or several lower-strength biaxial geogrid layers, often with a cushion layer or nonwoven geotextile over the column tops.
sections.body: Granular material (3.2.1.1, p. 6-16): if a soil layer just below the ground surface is stiff enough and deep enough, it may act as the LTP; otherwise backfill is needed. Arching in the LTP soil above the columns is integral to stress transfer, so the soil in the arching zone should be frictional material with high shear strength. Well graded granular fill is ideal; non-select fill may be used above the platform for the rest of the embankment. Geosynthetic reinforcement (3.2.1.2, p. 6-17): typically either a single layer of high strength geotextile or geogrid, or several layers of lower strength biaxial geogrid. Type and strength depend on the design model (catenary or beam), column spacing and embankment height. Many designers require a cushion layer of fill between the column tops and the reinforcement, or a nonwoven needle-punched geotextile between pile top and geogrid, to eliminate abrasion and reduce stress concentrations; pile caps should have rounded, not sharp, edges.
key_points: Arching-zone fill must be frictional with high shear strength; well graded granular fill is ideal.
Reinforcement: one high-strength geotextile/geogrid layer or several lower-strength biaxial geogrid layers.
A cushion layer or nonwoven geotextile over column tops reduces abrasion and stress concentration.
Pile caps should have rounded edges.
sections.applicability: Selecting LTP fill and geosynthetic reinforcement.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: LTP construction: roll reinforcement in the direction shown on drawings, remove wrinkles and slack, keep equipment off the geosynthetic with at least 6 in. of fill, consider seam type in design, and set compaction requirements and the first reinforcement level considering soft subgrade.
sections.body: Geosynthetic reinforcement should be rolled out in the direction indicated on the construction drawings (Figure 6-6). All wrinkles and slack should be removed before fill placement. No construction equipment should travel directly on the reinforcement, and a minimum of 6 inches of fill should be placed between the reinforcement and any equipment. Seam requirements shall be considered in design and selection of the reinforcement; LTPs to date have used both sewn and overlap seams. The select fill (Figure 6-7) should meet project requirements (Section 5 specifications). Compaction requirements should consider existing ground conditions: over soft subgrade it will be difficult to achieve 95% compaction in the first lift of select fill, though later lifts should reach it; the location of the first reinforcement layer should take this into account, and a reinforcement layer at subgrade helps achieve compaction in the first lift over soft subgrade (pp. 6-17 to 6-18).
key_points: Remove wrinkles and slack; no equipment directly on the geosynthetic; at least 6 in. of fill under equipment.
Sewn and overlap seams have both been used; consider seam type in design.
95% compaction is hard to achieve in the first lift over soft subgrade; a reinforcement layer at subgrade helps.

sections.title: Design Concepts
sections.summary: U.S. CSE design has moved from the semi-empirical beam method to the load and displacement compatibility (LDC) method (Sloan et al. 2013); the beam method remains for preliminary LTP sizing, and 2D/3D numerical analyses are also used with care.
sections.body: CSE design has advanced significantly in the last decade. The early U.S. method was the beam method, a semi-empirical method developed from laboratory testing and observed full-scale performance; it was instrumental in advancing the technology as an easy, straightforward method. Today it is being replaced by the more analytically correct load and displacement compatibility (LDC) method (Sloan et al. 2013). For preliminary designs the beam method is still used to determine LTP thickness and reinforcement. For final design, once a geosynthetic reinforced LTP is found to be required, reinforcement properties may be based on the preliminary beam design with the settlement analysis performed using the LDC method. The LDC method is discussed in detail; the beam method is in Section 4.7. Some specialty contractors and consultants perform 2D and 3D numerical deformation analyses; many finite element and finite difference programs are available, but great care and experience are needed to develop a reliable model, select input parameters and perform quality control checks (p. 6-19).
key_points: The LDC method (Sloan et al. 2013) is replacing the beam method.
Beam method still used for preliminary LTP thickness and reinforcement; LDC for final settlement analysis.
Numerical modeling requires great care, experience and quality control.
sections.applicability: Choosing a design approach for column-supported embankments.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: CSE design must address strength limit states (column capacity, lateral extent, vertical load transfer, lateral sliding, global stability) and serviceability (reinforcement strain typically limited to 5 to 6%, column settlement). Gives the 13 general design steps from preliminary spacing to construction observation.
sections.body: CSE design must consider strength limit states and serviceability state criteria. The limit state failure modes (Figure 6-8, after BS8006 2010) are: columns carrying the vertical embankment load without failing (typically assumed to carry the full load); the lateral extent of columns needed to prevent slides at the toe beyond the outermost column; the foundation soil and/or LTP transferring vertical load to the columns; lateral sliding of the embankment on top of the columns; and global stability. For serviceability, strain in the LTP geosynthetic should be kept below a maximum threshold, typically 5 to 6%, to preclude unacceptable differential settlement at the top of the embankment, and column settlement must be analyzed (Figure 6-9). General design steps (pp. 6-21 to 6-22): 1. estimate preliminary column spacing (Section 2.3); 2. determine required column load; 3. select a preliminary column type; 4. determine column capacity for limit and serviceability states; 5. determine the extent of columns across the embankment width; 6. check critical embankment height and adjust spacing; 7. determine if an LTP is required; 8. if reinforced, determine reinforcement requirements from the spacing and revise spacing as required; 9. determine reinforcement for lateral spreading; 10. determine overall reinforcement requirements; 11. check global stability; 12. prepare drawings and specifications; 13. observe construction.
key_points: Limit states: column capacity, lateral extent, vertical load transfer, lateral sliding, global stability.
Serviceability: geosynthetic strain typically kept below 5 to 6%; check column settlement.
Thirteen general design steps, from preliminary spacing to construction observation.
