sections.title: Design CSE with or without LTP
sections.summary: The trend has shifted from geosynthetic reinforced LTPs to unreinforced LTPs or no LTP; the chapter's design method applies to all three conditions, with the choice made on serviceability and economics. An LTP is a very small cost component of the overall system.
sections.body: CSE design has changed significantly over the last decade. In the previous version of the manual CSEs were designed almost exclusively with geosynthetic reinforced LTPs; the trend now is to design them with unreinforced LTPs or without an LTP altogether. The design methodology in the chapter is valid for all three conditions: no LTP, unreinforced LTP and reinforced LTP. The appropriate solution is selected on serviceability and economics, i.e., whether it meets the project settlement criteria and whether a solution without an LTP is more economical than one with an LTP that allows fewer columns at wider spacing. An LTP, reinforced or unreinforced, is a very small cost component of the overall system (p. 6-22).
key_points: The design method applies with no LTP, an unreinforced LTP or a reinforced LTP.
Choice is based on settlement criteria and economics.
An LTP is a very small cost component of the system.
sections.applicability: Deciding whether a CSE needs an LTP and whether to reinforce it.

sections.title: Column Design
sections.summary: Column load is based on tributary area, with embankment and surcharge carried entirely by the columns. The equivalent tributary diameter is 1.13 s for square and 1.05 s for triangular patterns; Eq. 6-1 gives the required nominal column load Qr. Typical loads are 25 to 75 kips at 5 ft spacing and 90 to 270 kips at 10 ft.
sections.body: Column type selection is most often based on constructability, load capacity versus stiffness, and cost. The required column load is typically based on the tributary area of each column, with the embankment and any surcharge assumed carried entirely by the columns. Figure 6-10 (Sloan et al. 2013) defines the unit cell: for a rectangular array Aunitcell = s1*s2 and s' = (s1^2+s2^2)^(1/2)/2 - d/2; for a triangular array Aunitcell = s1(s2^2 - s1^2/4)^(1/2) and s' = (s2^2+2s1^2)^(1/2)/3 - d/2; round column Ac = pi d^2/4, p = pi d; square column Ac = a^2, p = 4a, with equal-area conversion a = 0.866d. The polygonal tributary area can be approximated by an equivalent circle: the effective diameter De is 1.13 times the center-to-center spacing for a square pattern and 1.05 times for a triangular pattern (typical spacing 5 to 10 feet). Qr from Eq. 6-1 is the unfactored (nominal) load. Required loads are about 25 to 75 kips at 5 feet spacing and about 90 to 270 kips at 10 feet spacing for embankment heights of 10 to 30 feet. Table 6-1 with site conditions, constraints and cost is used to select a column type. Driven piles follow GEC 12 (2016), timber piles also Collin (2002), CFA piles GEC 8 (2007); cement based column capacity is typically designed by the contractor and verified with a static load test (pp. 6-22 to 6-24).
key_points: Embankment and surcharge loads are assumed carried entirely by the columns.
Effective tributary diameter De = 1.13 s (square) or 1.05 s (triangular).
Surcharge q typically 250 psf.
Qr is unfactored: about 25 to 75 kips at 5 ft spacing and 90 to 270 kips at 10 ft spacing for H = 10 to 30 ft.
Equal-area square-round conversion a = 0.866d.
equations: Eq. 6-1: Qr = pi (De/2)^2 (gamma H + q); required design vertical (nominal) load in the column, with De = effective tributary area diameter, H = embankment height, q = live and dead load surcharge (typically 250 psf), gamma = embankment unit weight
figures: Figure 6-10: Column layout and definition sketch for inputs to critical height and adapted Terzaghi method.
sections.applicability: Computing required column load for a CSE from tributary area.

sections.title: Lateral Extent of Columns
sections.summary: Columns must extend close enough to the embankment edge that instability or settlement outside the supported area is not a problem; ReSSA can check edge stability, and BS8006 (2010) requires columns within a distance Lp of the toe given by Eq. 6-2.
sections.body: The lateral extent of the column system should reach sufficiently close to the embankment edge to ensure that any instability or differential settlement outside the column supported area will not be problematic (Figure 6-8b). Several approaches can check edge stability; the FHWA software ReSSA, for reinforced and unreinforced slopes and embankments, is an excellent tool. BS8006 (2010) requires that the columns extend to within a minimum distance Lp of the embankment toe so that settlement of the unsupported edge does not affect the crest (Figure 6-11). In Eq. 6-2, n is the embankment side slope, theta_p is the angle from vertical between the outer edge of the outermost column and the crest of the embankment, theta_p = (45 - phi_emb/2), and phi_emb is the effective friction angle of the embankment fill (pp. 6-24 to 6-25).
key_points: ReSSA is suggested for checking edge stability.
BS8006 (2010): columns extend to within Lp of the toe.
theta_p = 45 - phi_emb/2, measured from vertical.
equations: Eq. 6-2: Lp = H (n - tan theta_p); BS8006 maximum distance from the embankment toe to the outer edge of the outermost column, with n = side slope, theta_p = 45 - phi_emb/2
figures: Figure 6-11: Lateral extent of columns.
sections.applicability: Setting how far columns extend under the embankment side slopes.

sections.title: Lateral Spreading
sections.summary: Lateral spreading force PLat (Eq. 6-3) is resisted by the foundation soil shear Rls = Ls Su (Eq. 6-4) with a recommended FS of 1.5; otherwise geosynthetic with long-term strength Tls >= PLat (Eq. 6-5) is added, anchored over length Le (Eq. 6-6).
sections.body: The potential for lateral spreading of the embankment must be analyzed (Figure 6-12). Resistance is provided by the shear strength of the foundation soils at the base of the embankment; if inadequate, geosynthetic reinforcement may be added instead of battered piles beneath the slope. This is critical because many vertical columns suitable for CSEs cannot provide adequate lateral resistance without failing. The required tensile force to prevent spreading PLat is given by Eq. 6-3, with Ka = tan^2(45 - phi_emb/2). Resistance without reinforcement is Eq. 6-4, with Su the undrained shear strength of the foundation soil and Ls the length of the side slope (Figure 6-11). A factor of safety Rls/PLat of 1.5 is recommended. If it cannot be achieved, a geosynthetic layer should be added; the reinforcement is typically designed to resist the entire PLat, with long-term design strength Tls greater than PLat (see GEC 11 (2009) for Tls), and multiple layers may be used. The minimum reinforcement length Le beyond the crest toward the toe, needed to develop the reinforcement strength without the side slope sliding across it, is Eq. 6-6, where ciemb is the coefficient of interaction for sliding between the geosynthetic and embankment fill (pp. 6-25 to 6-27).
key_points: Many vertical columns cannot resist lateral spreading without failing; use soil shear or geosynthetic rather than battered piles.
Recommended factor of safety for lateral spreading Rls/PLat = 1.5.
Reinforcement typically designed for the entire PLat; Tls per GEC 11 (2009).
equations: Eq. 6-3: PLat = Ka [gamma (H^2/2) + q H]; required tensile force to prevent lateral spreading, Ka = tan^2(45 - phi_emb/2)
Eq. 6-4: Rls = (Ls) Su; resistance to lateral spreading without geosynthetic, Ls = side slope length, Su = undrained shear strength of foundation soil
Eq. 6-5: Tls >= PLat; reinforcement long-term design strength must be at least the lateral spreading force
Eq. 6-6: Le = PLat / (0.5 gamma H ciemb tan phi_emb); minimum reinforcement length beyond the crest toward the toe
figures: Figure 6-12: Lateral spreading.
sections.applicability: Checking and reinforcing a CSE against lateral spreading.

sections.title: Critical Height
sections.summary: Critical height is the embankment height above which differential settlement at the CSE base produces no measurable differential settlement at the surface. Eq. 6-7 takes the larger of 1.5(s-a) and 1.15s'+1.44d; Eqs. 6-8 to 6-10 give maximum spacing for square, isosceles and equilateral arrays.
sections.body: Avoiding differential surface settlement matters for ride quality and overlying structures. It is influenced by column spacing and diameter, embankment height, subgrade support relative to column stiffness, and surface loading; it is likely for a low embankment with wide spacing and poor subgrade support. In this chapter critical height is the embankment height above which differential settlements at the base of the CSE do not produce measurable differential settlement at the surface, similar to Naughton's (2007) usage; others (Horgan and Sarsby 2002; Chen et al. 2008) define it as the height above which all additional fill and surcharge load goes completely to the pile caps. For CSEs without subgrade support, McGuire (2011) found Hcrit depends on column diameter and spacing, not significantly on fill relative density or geosynthetic reinforcement: Hcrit = 1.15s' + 1.44d (s' per Figure 6-10). Sloan's (2011) field tests agree with this and with the conventional Hcrit = 1.5(s - a) for square arrays. The GeoTechTools approach uses the larger of the two (Eq. 6-7). Where a square array of square pile caps is used and the embankment height is fixed, the column spacing can be estimated by Eq. 6-8; for round caps 0.886d (as printed) can be substituted for the cap width a. Eqs. 6-9 and 6-10 are for isosceles and equilateral triangular arrays (pp. 6-27 to 6-28).
key_points: Critical height: height above which base differential settlement gives no measurable surface differential settlement.
Hcrit = max{1.5(s - a), 1.15s' + 1.44d}; the embankment height H must exceed it.
Spacing limits: s <= 1.2(H - a) square, 1.4(H - a) isosceles triangular, 1.5(H - a) equilateral triangular.
equations: Eq. 6-7: H > Hcrit = max{1.5(s - a); 1.15s' + 1.44d}; critical embankment height
Eq. 6-8: s <= 1.2(H - a); column spacing for a square array of square pile caps
Eq. 6-9: s <= 1.4(H - a); column spacing for an isosceles triangular array
Eq. 6-10: s <= 1.5(H - a); column spacing for an equilateral triangular array
sections.applicability: Checking embankment height against column spacing to avoid surface differential settlement.

sections.title: Load Transfer Platform Design
sections.summary: Describes the load and displacement compatibility (LDC) method (Smith 2005; Filz and Smith 2006, 2007) for loads on the LTP and reinforcement: vertical equilibrium (Eq. 6-11) with displacement compatibility in an axisymmetric unit cell, solved in the GeogridBridge spreadsheet; applicable to reinforced and unreinforced LTPs.
sections.body: There are over a dozen methods to design the LTP; the practical one modeling the actual load transfer is the load displacement compatibility (LDC) method, developed by Smith (2005) and Filz and Smith (2006, 2007) and usable for unreinforced LTPs too. Its features: vertical equilibrium and displacement compatibility at the reinforcement level to distribute load among columns, soil, geosynthetic and embankment base; an axisymmetric unit cell for vertical load on the geosynthetic; a 3D representation and parabolic deformation between columns for tension (as in BS8006 2010); round columns or square caps in a square array; embankment response linear up to a limit state set by the Adapted Terzaghi Method; linear-elastic geosynthetic with nonlinear load-deflection from large displacement; clay between columns modeled with compression ratio, recompression ratio and preconsolidation pressure; and slippage at the soil-column interface. The embankment-around-column relation uses an elastic circular-load solution (Poulos and Davis 1974) up to the limit given by the Adapted Terzaghi Method (Russell and Pierpoint 1997) with K = 0.75. Column compression uses a constant modulus; if voids are expected under the LTP, ignore foundation soil support. Soil sheds load to the column by interface friction until column and soil settlements are equal; maximum differential settlement at subgrade is taken as twice the average (Russell et al. 2003), judged conservative. The equations are implemented in the GeogridBridge spreadsheet (Filz and Smith 2006) on GeoTechTools, which allows two fill types, J = 0 for no reinforcement, column properties varying with depth, two sand and two clay layers, and automatic solution. The method was validated against numerical analyses and case histories (Filz and Smith 2007; McGuire et al. 2009), pp. 6-28 to 6-33.
key_points: LDC method applies to reinforced and unreinforced LTPs.
Limiting embankment stress from the Adapted Terzaghi Method with K = 0.75.
Maximum differential settlement at subgrade taken as twice the average (Russell et al. 2003), a conservative approximation.
GeogridBridge spreadsheet solves the equations; set J = 0 for no geosynthetic.
If voids may form beneath the LTP, ignore subgrade support.
equations: Eq. 6-11: gamma H + q = as sigma_col,geotop + (1 - as) sigma_soil,geotop = as sigma_col,geobot + (1 + as) sigma_soil,geobot (as printed); vertical equilibrium of the unit cell, as = Ac/Aunitcell area replacement ratio
figures: Figure 6-13: Definition sketch for load and displacement compatibility (LDC) method.
sections.applicability: Analyzing load transfer and settlement of a CSE load transfer platform.

sections.title: Generalized Adapted Terzaghi Method
sections.summary: Generalized Adapted Terzaghi Method for the limiting stress on the embankment base over soil: any column arrangement and cap area, up to two fill layers, and vertical shearing limited to below Hcrit. Parameter alpha (Eq. 6-12) and stress sigma_soil for three cases of H1, H2 and Hcrit (Eqs. 6-13 to 6-15).
sections.body: The Adapted Terzaghi Method for the limiting distribution of stress acting up on the base of the embankment agrees reasonably with numerical analyses and case histories (Russell and Pierpoint 1997; Filz and Smith 2006), with other rational methods (Hewlett and Randolph 1988; Kempfert et al. 2004a, 2004b, per McGuire and Filz 2008) and with Sloan's (2011) field tests, and is relatively simple. As presented by Russell and Pierpoint (1997) and Russell et al. (2003) it applies to a square arrangement of square columns and one fill. The generalized version accommodates any column arrangement and cap area (Figure 6-10); up to two embankment fill layers (an LTP fill and a lower quality fill above), differing in unit weight, friction angle and lateral earth pressure coefficient; and vertical shearing limited to the embankment below the critical height, with the weight above treated as surcharge (Filz and Smith 2006; Sloan et al. 2011). Inputs: H1,2 layer thicknesses (Figure 6-2), gamma1,2, K1,2, phi1,2, surcharge q, perimeter p, Aunitcell, Ac and Asoil = Aunitcell - Ac. The average upward stress on the embankment base over soil (sigma_soil,geotop, or sigma_soil without geosynthetic) is Eq. 6-13 for H1 + H2 <= Hcrit, Eq. 6-14 for H1 <= Hcrit <= H1 + H2, and Eq. 6-15 for Hcrit <= H1 (pp. 6-33 to 6-34).
key_points: Generalized for any column arrangement, cap area and up to two fill layers.
Vertical shearing limited to below the critical height; fill above treated as surcharge.
Asoil = Aunitcell - Ac.
equations: Eq. 6-12: alpha1,2 = p K1,2 tan phi1,2 / Asoil; combined parameter for each fill layer

Eq. 6-13: sigma_soil = (gamma1/alpha1)(1 - e^(-alpha1 H1)) + (gamma2/alpha2)(e^(-alpha1 H1))(1 - e^(-alpha2 H2)) + q (e^(-alpha1 H1))(e^(-alpha2 H2)); limiting stress on base over soil for H1 + H2 <= Hcrit

Eq. 6-14: sigma_soil = (gamma1/alpha1)(1 - e^(-alpha1 H1)) + (gamma2/alpha2)(e^(-alpha1 H1))(1 - e^(-alpha2 (Hcrit - H1))) + [q + (H1 + H2 - Hcrit) gamma2](e^(-alpha1 H1))(e^(-alpha2 (Hcrit - H1))); for H1 <= Hcrit <= H1 + H2
Eq. 6-15: sigma_soil = (gamma1/alpha1)(1 - e^(-alpha1 Hcrit)) + [q + (H1 - Hcrit) gamma1 + H2 gamma2](e^(-alpha1 H1)) (exponent as printed); for Hcrit <= H1
sections.applicability: Computing the limiting arching stress on the subgrade between CSE columns.

sections.title: Generalized Parabolic Method
sections.summary: Generalized parabolic method (BS8006 2010 with stress-strain compatibility, Filz and Smith 2006; adapted by Sloan 2011) for geogrid tension: Eq. 6-16 for biaxial geogrid over rectangular arrays with 0.5 <= s1/s2 <= 2, and Eq. 6-17 for biaxial geogrid over triangular arrays.
sections.body: At least three methods calculate tension in CSE geosynthetic reinforcement: the parabolic method (BS8006 2010), the tensioned membrane method (Collin 2004, 2007) and the embedded membrane method (Kempfert et al. 2004a, 2004b). The parabolic method agrees well with numerical analyses (Filz and Plaut 2009) and Sloan's (2011) field tests. BS8006 applies it to square caps in a square array without stress-strain compatibility; Filz and Smith (2006) added compatibility and Sloan (2011) adapted it to the Figure 6-10 geometries. For biaxial geogrid aligned with a rectangular array the solution is Eq. 6-16, where T is geogrid tension, sigma_net = sigma_soil,geotop - sigma_soil,geobot is the net vertical stress on the geogrid, Asoil is the geogrid area in a unit cell underlain by soil (Asoil = Ap in Figure 6-14), p is the column or cap perimeter and J the sum of the geogrid layer stiffnesses. Typically two to four geogrid layers are used, each rotated 90 degrees, so an average J is justified. Strain is epsilon = T/J. Eq. 6-16 is recommended for rectangular arrays with 0.5 <= s1/s2 <= 2, including square arrays, and (the print says Equation 6-10) also applies to radially isotropic geogrids over rectangular or triangular arrays in that range. For biaxial geogrid over a triangular array the solution, based on the assumptions in Figure 6-14, is Eq. 6-17, solved simultaneously for T1 and T2, with epsilon1 = T1/J1 and epsilon2 = T2/J2 (pp. 6-34 to 6-36).
key_points: Parabolic method agrees well with numerical analyses (Filz and Plaut 2009) and field tests (Sloan 2011).
Typically two to four geogrid layers, each rotated 90 degrees; J is the sum of layer stiffnesses.
Eq. 6-16 valid for 0.5 <= s1/s2 <= 2; strain epsilon = T/J.
equations: Eq. 6-16: 6T^3 - 6T(sigma_net Asoil/p)^2 - J(sigma_net Asoil/p)^2 = 0; geogrid tension for biaxial geogrid aligned with a rectangular column array
Eq. 6-17: 2aT1/sqrt(1 + J1/(6T1)) + 2aT2/sqrt(1 + J2/(6T2)) - sigma_net Asoil = 0 and T1 c1^2/J1 = T2 c2^2/J2; geogrid tensions for biaxial geogrid over a triangular column array
figures: Figure 6-14: Triangular column arrangements with biaxial geogrid.
sections.applicability: Computing geogrid tension and strain in a reinforced LTP.

sections.title: Geosynthetic Properties
sections.summary: LTP design uses the long-term stiffness J (serviceability), taken from the isochronous creep curve at the design life and design strain, not from quick tests such as ASTM D6637, and the available long-term strength (strength state), the short-term strength divided by creep, installation damage and durability reduction factors (GEC 11 Chapter 3).
sections.body: The two geosynthetic values used in LTP design are the stiffness J and the available long-term strength, relating to the serviceability state and strength state respectively. J should be the long-term stiffness, not the load-displacement relationship from quick (short-term) tests such as ASTM D6637. J for LTP design is defined at the specified or selected design life and the reinforcement design strain: the isochronous creep curve at the design life (e.g., 50 or 75 years) defines J as the tensile strength corresponding to the design strain. The available long-term strength is the quick (short-term) tensile strength (e.g., ASTM D6637) divided by the product of creep, installation damage and durability reduction factors; the procedures are well established in Chapter 3 of GEC 11 (2009), pp. 6-36 to 6-37.
key_points: Stiffness J: long-term, from the isochronous creep curve at the design life and design strain.
Long-term strength: short-term strength divided by the product of creep, installation damage and durability reduction factors.
Do not use quick-test (ASTM D6637) load-displacement as J.
sections.applicability: Selecting geosynthetic stiffness and strength values for LTP design.

sections.title: Beam Method
sections.summary: The semi-empirical beam method for preliminary LTP design: LTP thickness at least half the clear span, three or more reinforcement layers at least 8 in. apart, initial strain limited to 5%. Layer loads by Eqs. 6-18/6-19 and tension by Eq. 6-20 with Omega from Table 6-2.
sections.body: The beam method is simple and often used for preliminary LTP design, for example when the soft subgrade is not characterized well enough for the LDC method. Assumptions (p. 6-37): LTP thickness h is at least one-half the clear span (1/2 (s - d)); a minimum of three layers of extensible (geosynthetic) reinforcement; minimum vertical spacing between layers of 8 inches; select fill in the LTP; reinforcement primarily provides lateral confinement to facilitate arching within the LTP and secondarily supports the soil wedge below the arch; all vertical load from the embankment above the LTP goes to the columns; initial reinforcement strain limited to 5%. The load carried by each layer depends on the column pattern (square or triangular) and the vertical spacing. If the subgrade can support the first lift, the first layer is placed 6 to 10 inches above subgrade. Each layer carries the LTP fill within the soil wedge below the arch between that layer and the next above (Figure 6-14 'Beam method', as numbered in print). WTn = ((area at layer n + area at layer n+1)/2)(layer thickness)(LTP fill density)/(area at layer n). Tension is from tension membrane theory (Giroud et al. 1990), Eq. 6-20, with D = design span: (s-d)n for square spacing or (s-d)n tan 30 degrees for triangular spacing, and Omega from Table 6-2 (Young et al. 2003): Omega = 2.07, 1.47, 1.23, 1.08, 0.97 for strain 1, 2, 3, 4, 5% (pp. 6-37 to 6-39).
key_points: LTP thickness h >= 1/2 (s - d); at least three reinforcement layers at least 8 in. apart.
Initial reinforcement strain limited to 5%.
First layer 6 to 10 in. above subgrade if the subgrade supports the first lift.
equations: Eq. 6-18: WTn = [(s - d)n^2 + (s - d)n+1^2] sin 60 deg (hn gamma / ((s - d)n^2 sin 60 deg)); uniform vertical load on reinforcement layer n for a triangular pattern
Eq. 6-19: WTn = [(s - d)n^2 + (s - d)n+1^2] (hn gamma / (s - d)n^2); uniform vertical load on reinforcement layer n for a square pattern
Eq. 6-20: Trpn = WTn Omega (D/2); tension in reinforcement layer n by tension membrane theory, D = design span
figures: Figure 6-14: Beam method.
sections.applicability: Preliminary design of a multi-layer reinforced LTP by the beam method.

sections.title: Reinforcement Total Design Load
sections.summary: Lateral spreading and LTP reinforcement have been designed separately or combined; because lateral spreading needs high strength in one direction and the LTP needs biaxial reinforcement, separate reinforcements are generally recommended. Allowable long-term strength is used for lateral spreading.
sections.body: Separate geosynthetic layers for lateral spreading and for the LTP have been used, or the two force requirements have been combined and one geosynthetic able to resist their sum used. The tensile strength for lateral spreading may be relatively high compared with the LTP requirement, and its load direction is perpendicular to the embankment, needing strength in one direction, while the LTP load is bi-directional, needing a biaxial geogrid or geotextile. For these reasons separate reinforcements are generally recommended for lateral spreading and for the LTP. The allowable long-term tensile strength of the geosynthetic is used in the lateral spreading computations; as in Section 4.6.3, it is the quick (short-term) tensile strength (e.g., ASTM D6637) divided by the product of creep, installation damage and durability reduction factors (pp. 6-39 to 6-40).
key_points: Separate reinforcements are generally recommended for lateral spreading (uniaxial) and the LTP (biaxial).
Use the allowable long-term tensile strength for lateral spreading.
sections.applicability: Combining or separating lateral spreading and LTP reinforcement.

sections.title: Global Stability
sections.summary: Global stability can be checked with limit equilibrium software including column shear resistance and geosynthetic tension (BS8006 approach, Figure 6-15); when load is effectively transferred to the firm layer, global stability is rarely a problem and analyses are not generally required.
sections.body: Global stability of CSEs may be evaluated with limit equilibrium computer software, considering the added shear resistance of the columns and the tensile capacity of the geosynthetic reinforcement. The British Standard approach for including the benefit of columns and geosynthetic is shown in the figure printed as Figure 6-15 (cited in the text as Figure 6-16). For incorporating the columns see Chapter 5 Aggregate Columns, and for geosynthetic reinforcement see GEC 11 (2009). When the embankment load is effectively transferred to the firm foundation soil below the soft layer using the procedures above, there is very small potential for a global stability problem, and global stability analyses are consequently not generally required (pp. 6-40 to 6-41).
key_points: Use limit equilibrium software including column shear resistance and geosynthetic tension.
With load effectively transferred to the firm layer, global stability analyses are not generally required.
figures: Figure 6-15: Variables used in global stability analysis.
sections.applicability: Global stability checks for column-supported embankments.

sections.title: Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Unless the agency has CSE design, construction and inspection expertise, a performance specification is good practice; an experienced agency may use a method specification.
sections.body: Like other specialty construction, unless the specifying agency has expertise in the design, construction and inspection of CSEs, it is good practice to specify the work under a performance type specification. If the agency has the necessary experience, a method specification may be used (p. 6-42).
key_points: Performance specification recommended unless the agency has CSE expertise.
sections.applicability: Choosing a specification approach for a CSE.

sections.title: CSE Performance Specification
sections.summary: Performance specifications cover design and installation of columns and LTP; a guide performance specification with commentary is on GeoTechTools. The specification defines failure modes and minimum factors of safety, leaves design methods to the contractor, and the agency should check the design using the LDC method.
sections.body: Performance specifications shall include design and installation of the columns and the LTP. Column specifications are beyond the chapter's scope: see GEC 12 (2016) for driven piles, the other chapters for soil mix and aggregate columns, and GeoTechTools for cement based columns. During development of GeoTechTools, CSE specifications were evaluated, including the method and performance specifications in the previous manual and a draft state DOT LTP specification; with project experience these produced the Column-Supported Embankment Performance Guide Specification, a complete specification with commentary and instructions adaptable to a project, available on the GeoTechTools Technology Information page for CSEs. The specification shall clearly define the failure modes to be analyzed in the design-build contractor's submittal and the required minimum factors of safety, but the choice of design methods should be left to the contractor. As part of approval, the specifying agency should check the contractor's design using the LDC method (p. 6-42).
key_points: A guide performance specification with commentary is available on GeoTechTools.
Specify failure modes and minimum factors of safety; leave design methods to the contractor.
The agency should check the contractor's design with the LDC method.
sections.applicability: Writing a performance specification for a CSE.

sections.title: LTP Method Specification
sections.summary: If the agency wants a specific LTP design approach, a method specification for the LTP complementary to the CSE performance specification, or a combined performance/method specification, may be used; a guide LTP method specification is on GeoTechTools.
sections.body: If the specifying agency wants a specific design approach for the load transfer platform, a method specification for the LTP that complements the CSE performance specification may be used. Alternatively, a combined performance/method specification for the CSE and LTP could be developed. A guide method specification for an LTP is available on the GeoTechTools Technology Information page for Column-Supported Embankments, and should be modified as appropriate for the particular project requirements (pp. 6-42 to 6-43).
key_points: An LTP method specification can complement the CSE performance specification.
A guide LTP method specification is on GeoTechTools.
sections.applicability: Specifying a particular LTP design approach.

sections.title: Quality Assurance
sections.summary: QC/QA for CSE: verify LTP fill, embankment fill and geosynthetic properties and placement; test sections only for very large projects or performance specifications; monitor settlement and lateral displacement. Lists geosynthetic, fill and monitoring checks, including lift thickness limits of 10 in. and 6 in.
sections.body: QC/QA should verify the properties and placement of the LTP fill, embankment fill and geosynthetic reinforcement. Very large projects may budget a test section, but the need has diminished with experience; settlement and/or lateral displacement monitoring should be included, and industry QC/QA for the column type followed. Pre-production test sections should be considered only on very large projects or with a performance specification, where monitoring becomes the basis for acceptance, typically minimum total and/or differential settlement criteria. Geosynthetic checks: document manufacturer, model, lot and roll numbers; verify certified ultimate strength (ASTM D6637 geogrid or D4595 geotextile), creep resistance (D5262), durability and coefficient of interaction for sliding (D5321); inspect each roll; avoid prolonged UV exposure; remove deleterious materials; verify the geosynthetic is taut unless sagging is prescribed; keep equipment off it until minimum fill is placed, with no sharp turns; avoid large fill piles on the LTP; verify orientation, overlap and elevation; seams placed up with every stitch inspected. Fill checks: gradation, Atterberg limits, modified Proctor or min/max density, in situ density, and maximum lift thickness (10 inches for large compaction equipment, 6 inches for hand operated). Monitoring: surface survey and periodic resurvey, settlement plates at the reinforcement elevation, and inclinometers at the toe (pp. 6-43 to 6-45).
key_points: Test sections only for very large projects or performance specifications.
Verify geosynthetic strength (ASTM D6637/D4595), creep (D5262) and interaction (D5321).
Maximum lift thickness: 10 in. for large compaction equipment, 6 in. for hand operated equipment.
Monitor with surface surveys, settlement plates at the reinforcement and inclinometers at the toe.
sections.applicability: Construction quality assurance and monitoring for CSEs.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Guidelines for budget estimates of the three main CSE cost components: the construction working platform (if required), the columns and the LTP, with GeoTechTools as an additional source.
sections.body: This section gives guidelines for preparing budget estimates so that the economic feasibility of a CSE can be evaluated, referring readers to GeoTechTools for further guidance on preliminary cost estimates. It provides cost information on the three main components of a CSE: the construction working platform (if required), the columns and the LTP (p. 6-46).
sections.applicability: Preliminary cost estimating for CSEs.

sections.title: Access and Mobility
sections.summary: Working platforms of geosynthetic and aggregate are often needed for equipment access; 2005 to 2010 DOT bids gave geosynthetic at $1.00 to $3.50/yd2 and granular fill at $7.00 to $20.00/ton delivered, with equipment and labor about equal to material cost.
sections.body: On many CSE sites the surface soils are so weak that a working platform is needed for equipment to move around. It typically consists of a geosynthetic reinforcement and a bridging layer of aggregate; its design is beyond the chapter's scope (see GeoTechTools and Chapter 9 Pavement Support Stabilization Technologies). Estimating its cost is straightforward. A review of DOT bids between 2005 and 2010 found geosynthetics for working platforms cost $1.00 to $3.50 per square yard including delivery, overlaps and waste, and granular fill $7.00 to $20.00 per ton delivered depending on region. Once the platform thickness is estimated, equipment and labor costs may be taken as about equal to the cost of the platform materials (p. 6-46).
key_points: Working platform geosynthetic: $1.00 to $3.50/yd2 (2005-2010 bids).
Granular fill: $7.00 to $20.00/ton delivered.
Equipment and labor about equal to material cost.
sections.applicability: Estimating working platform cost for a CSE site.

sections.title: Column Cost
sections.summary: Table 6-1 information can be used for a preliminary column cost estimate for production installation; mobilization, verification load tests and quality assurance testing and observation should be added.
sections.body: Information in Table 6-1 can be used to perform a preliminary estimate of the cost of the columns. The unit cost is for production column installation. Additional costs to consider are mobilization and column verification load tests; quality assurance testing and observation should also be considered (p. 6-46).
key_points: Add mobilization, verification load tests and QA to production column cost.
sections.applicability: Preliminary column cost estimate for a CSE.

sections.title: LTP Cost
sections.summary: LTP costs: reinforcement $8.35 to $12.00/yd2 (2005-2010 projects), granular fill $7.00 to $20.00/ton, thickness about (s-d)/2, labor about equal to materials. The worked estimate for 10 ft spacing and 20 in. columns gives a total of $76/yd2 of LTP plan area.
sections.body: LTP components are the geosynthetic reinforcement, the select LTP fill and the labor to install them. Reinforcement used on several projects built between 2005 and 2010 cost $8.35 to $12.00/yd2 including delivery, overlaps and waste; granular fill $7.00 to $20.00 per ton delivered depending on region. For preliminary cost the LTP thickness may be taken as one-half the clear spacing between columns, (s - d)/2, and equipment and labor costs as about equal to material costs. Printed example (p. 6-47) for 10 ft spacing, 20-inch columns, $10.00/yd2 reinforcement and $12.00/ton select fill: reinforcement $10/yd2; thickness (10 - 1.67)/2 = 4.1 ft; fill weight (4.1 ft)(125 pcf) = 520 psf; fill cost (520 psf)($6/1,000 lbs) = $3.12/ft2, about $28/yd2; material $38/yd2; labor $38/yd2; total $76/yd2 of LTP plan area (pp. 6-46 to 6-47).
key_points: LTP reinforcement $8.35 to $12.00/yd2 (2005-2010).
Preliminary LTP thickness = (s - d)/2.
Worked estimate: 4.1 ft thick LTP, total $76/yd2 of LTP plan area.
sections.applicability: Estimating LTP cost for a CSE.

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: Introduces the chapter's two case histories of column-supported embankments at bridge approaches: controlled modulus columns under MSE walls, and capped steel pipe piles under a tall embankment.
sections.body: This section presents the manual's two case histories: controlled modulus column support of an MSE-walled bridge approach widening (7.1) and a pipe-pile CSE beneath a tall bridge approach embankment (7.2), pp. 6-48 to 6-55.
sections.applicability: Field examples of CSE design and construction.

sections.title: Case History: CMC-Supported MSE Wall Approaches for a Bridge Widening
sections.summary: The manual's first case history: widening bridge approaches from two to three lanes with MSE walls, where controlled modulus columns (CMCs) replaced the specified stone columns as a value-engineered alternative, completed in 2010.
sections.body: This is the manual's first case history (printed section 7.1, p. 6-48), a parkway bridge approach widening constructed in 2010. The printed heading names the project; its basic information lists the location, owner, engineer, contractor, ground modification subcontractor and year constructed (2010).
key_points: Constructed 2010.
Controlled modulus columns supported MSE walls for a bridge approach widening.
sections.applicability: Case history of CMCs under MSE wall bridge approaches.

sections.title: Project Summary
sections.summary: Widening approaches from two to three lanes with a two-stage MSE wall originally on stone columns; a value-engineered CMC alternative allowed a one-stage wall, designed with a large 3D finite element model and supporting 2D models.
sections.body: When the roadway approaches to the bridge were widened from two to three lanes, a two-stage MSE retaining wall was designed to support the embankment and minimize encroachment on wetlands, with stone columns specified as ground improvement under the walls. The ground modification subcontractor proposed a value-engineered alternative using Controlled Modulus Columns (CMCs) instead of stone columns, which allowed a one-stage MSE wall instead of a two-stage wall; the owner and general contractor selected it. The CMC design used a large-scale 3D finite element model with several supporting 2D finite element models (Figure 6-17), which helped optimize the design and meet the target performance requirements (pp. 6-48 to 6-49).
key_points: CMCs replaced stone columns, allowing a one-stage instead of two-stage MSE wall.
Design used a large-scale 3D finite element model with supporting 2D models.
figures: Figure 6-17: 3D numerical model of MSE wall and CMCs.
sections.applicability: Value engineering of CSE columns for an MSE wall widening.

sections.title: Ground Conditions
sections.summary: Variable profile of controlled embankment fill over organics and sand; columns installed through the organics into dense sand at depths of 25 to 50 ft.
sections.body: The site had a variable soil profile, with varying depths of controlled embankment fill in the upper layers, underlain by organics and sand below. The columns were installed through the organics and founded in the dense sand at depth. Column depths varied from 25 to 50 feet (p. 6-49).
key_points: Column depths 25 to 50 ft, founded in dense sand below organics.
sections.applicability: Ground conditions of the first CSE case history.

sections.title: Ground Modification Solution
sections.summary: CMCs treated 1,400 linear ft of MSE wall on the south approach and 2,600 ft on the north, about 126,000 ft2 in total, with 2,129 columns installed in two phases; completed on schedule in summer 2010.
sections.body: CMCs were used for ground modification of 1,400 linear feet of MSE wall on the south approach and 2,600 linear feet on the north approach, a total treatment area of approximately 126,000 square feet. A total of 2,129 columns were installed in two phases (Figure 6-18). In phase one, columns were installed from a lower elevation in the strip zone of the MSE walls; after the wall was partially built, the remaining columns were installed from a higher elevation for embankment support. The MSE walls were designed by the wall system supplier. The ground modification was completed on schedule in the summer of 2010 (pp. 6-49 to 6-50).
key_points: 1,400 ft (south) and 2,600 ft (north) of MSE wall; about 126,000 ft2 treated.
2,129 CMCs installed in two phases.
figures: Figure 6-18: CMC installation Phase 2.
sections.applicability: Phased CMC installation under MSE walls.

sections.title: Case History: Bridge over a River, Pipe-Pile CSE Approach Embankment
sections.summary: The manual's second case history: a 35 ft approach embankment for a design-build bridge over a river, on six strata with deep compressible clay loam, supported on a CSE of open-ended steel pipe piles with concrete pile caps and a geogrid reinforced LTP, built 2010 and 2011 and instrumented.
sections.body: The basic information for the bridge over the river (the manual's second case history, printed section 7.2, p. 6-50, whose heading names the bridge and river) is as follows: project location; owner: a state department of transportation; CSE engineer; contractor: a joint venture; year constructed: 2010-2014 (CSE was constructed in 2010 and 2011). The subsections give the project summary (a 35-foot tall approach embankment over multiple deep compressible strata), the ground conditions (six strata, Table 6-3) and the ground modification solution (open-ended steel pipe piles with pile caps, a load transfer platform with biaxial geogrid, and instrumentation), pp. 6-50 to 6-55.
key_points: Year constructed 2010-2014; the CSE was constructed in 2010 and 2011.
Steel pipe pile columns with pile caps and a geogrid reinforced LTP under a 35 ft embankment.
sections.applicability: Case history of a steel pipe pile CSE under a tall bridge approach embankment.

sections.title: Project Summary
sections.summary: A $130M design-build replacement bridge completed in 2014; a 35 ft tall approach embankment over multiple deep compressible strata needed ground modification for serviceability, global stability and schedule, and the team chose a CSE.
sections.body: A $130M design-build replacement bridge project was completed in 2014, carrying four lanes of traffic and a pedestrian trail over a river. A 35-foot tall approach embankment adjacent to the existing bridge embankment on the north side was in an area with multiple deep compressible strata (Figure 6-19). Strict performance requirements for serviceability and global stability, combined with a tight construction schedule, dictated ground modification beneath the embankment, and after evaluating several alternatives the design-build team elected to design and construct a CSE (p. 6-51).
key_points: 35 ft tall approach embankment over multiple deep compressible strata.
Serviceability, global stability and schedule led to a CSE.
figures: Figure 6-19: Cross section of column supported approach embankment (case history 7.2).
sections.applicability: Project setting for the second CSE case history.

sections.title: Ground Conditions
sections.summary: Six strata (Table 6-3): mixed sand-silt-clay to 50 ft, organic silty clay loam 50 to 110 ft, sand with gravel 110 to 125 ft, organic silty clay loam 125 to 150 ft, sand with gravel 150 to 185 ft, bedrock below 185 ft; columns tipped about 155 ft below grade; groundwater about 7 ft deep.
sections.body: The site stratigraphy consists of six strata (Table 6-3, p. 6-51), with average N60 (blows/ft) and depth from existing grade: I mixture of sand, silt and clay, N60 15, 0 to 50 ft; II slightly organic silty clay loam, 9, 50 to 110 ft; III sand with some gravel, 50, 110 to 125 ft; IV slightly organic silty clay loam, 11, 125 to 150 ft; V sand with some gravel, 75+, 150 to 185 ft; VI bedrock, 185+ ft. Strata II and IV and the fine-grained layers in Stratum I have very high natural moisture contents and relatively low shear strength; they would settle excessively under the full embankment load without mitigation and give unacceptably low global stability factors of safety. Strata III and V are medium dense to very dense coarse-grained layers with moderate moisture and relatively high shear strength. The CSE columns were tipped near the top of Stratum V, about 155 feet below existing grade. Groundwater was near the river elevation, about 7 feet below existing grade in non-flood conditions.
key_points: Compressible strata II (50-110 ft) and IV (125-150 ft) with N60 9 and 11.
Columns tipped near the top of Stratum V, about 155 ft below grade.
Groundwater about 7 ft below existing grade.
tables: Table 6-3: Brief Summary of Project Stratigraphy (case history 7.2)
sections.applicability: Subsurface conditions of the second CSE case history.

sections.title: Ground Modification Solution
sections.summary: The CSE used 12.75 in. O.D. open-ended steel pipe piles on a 10 ft square grid with 5 ft diameter reinforced concrete caps and an LTP of select granular fill with three biaxial geogrid levels, designed per Collin (2007); columns designed by alpha and beta methods to a required tip elevation, and instrumented.
sections.body: A CSE was the primary settlement and stability mitigation, selected to protect the schedule relative to preloading or surcharging, avoid reliance on specialty subcontractors, reach the depth of improvement needed for stringent performance requirements, and provide a robust, reliable and economical system for the 100-year design life. Alternatives considered included extending the bridge, lightweight fill, preloading and surcharge, in situ mixing with cementitious materials and other column types; schedule, cost, reliability and the ability to self-perform led to the choice. The CSE used 12.75-inch O.D. open-ended steel pipe piles on a 10-foot center-to-center square grid, with an LTP of well-compacted free-draining select granular fill reinforced with three levels of biaxial geogrid (Figure 6-20). To reduce the span and LTP thickness, 5-foot diameter reinforced concrete caps were placed on each pile (Figure 6-21). The LTP was designed in general accordance with the Collin Method (Collin 2007); the columns by the alpha method in fine-grained soils and the beta method in sand layers, installed to a required tip elevation since their purpose was settlement control, which requires an extensive subsurface investigation (rotary borings and CPTu). Piles were installed with open-ended diesel hammers. Instrumentation (borehole settlement devices, piezometers, column strain gages, wall tiltmeters): piezometers, strain gages and tiltmeters worked well; multiple borehole settlement devices in single holes gave questionable data, and horizontal shape accelerometer arrays (SAA) are considered superior for future settlement monitoring (pp. 6-53 to 6-55).
key_points: 12.75 in. O.D. open-ended steel pipe piles at 10 ft square spacing with 5 ft diameter concrete caps.
LTP of select granular fill with three levels of biaxial geogrid, designed per Collin (2007).
Columns installed to a required tip elevation for settlement control.
Horizontal shape accelerometer arrays recommended over stacked borehole settlement devices.

sections.title: Example Problems
sections.summary: Introduces two worked CSE example problems: a full design of a 20.5 ft MSE-walled approach embankment over 20 ft of soft clay, and a variant with 5 ft of sand at subgrade analyzing only the bridging layer decision.
sections.body: This section presents two worked examples (pp. 6-56 to 6-67). Example Problem 1 steps through the general design procedure for a column-supported approach embankment over soft clay; Example Problem 2 repeats the bridging-layer step for a profile with a sand layer at subgrade.
sections.applicability: Worked examples applying the CSE design steps.

sections.title: Example Problem 1
sections.summary: Example 1 designs a CSE for a 20.5 ft high MSE-walled approach embankment over 20 ft of soft clay using the 12-step procedure, ending with 7 ft triangular spacing of 3 ft VCCs, a 3 ft bridging layer with two geogrid layers, and lateral spreading geosynthetic.
sections.body: Example Problem 1 (pp. 6-56 to 6-64) applies the general design steps to a 20.5-foot high approach embankment on 20 feet of soft clay with MSE walls on both sides. It is presented as a problem statement (8.1.1) and a solution in twelve steps (8.1.2).
sections.applicability: Complete worked design of a column-supported embankment.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.summary: A 20.5 ft high, 60 ft wide approach embankment retained by MSE walls (15 ft reinforcement) over 20 ft of soft clay (Su 250 psf, Cc ratio 0.18), groundwater 3 ft deep; paving at 60 days with a maximum post-pavement settlement of 2.5 in.
sections.body: A 20.5-foot high approach embankment is to be built over a 20-foot thick soft compressible clay layer with groundwater 3 feet below grade; time constraints led to a CSE. Soft clay: thickness 20 ft, unit weight 100 pcf, undrained shear strength 250 lb/ft2, Poisson's ratio 0.3, effective friction angle 24 degrees, at-rest coefficient 0.6, compression ratio 0.18, recompression ratio 0.01, coefficient of consolidation 0.35 ft2/day. Embankment fill (silty sand): 115 pcf, Poisson's ratio 0.33, phi' 30 degrees, Ka 0.33, Young's modulus 350,000 psf. Bridging layer (dense graded aggregate): 130 pcf, phi' 40 degrees, Young's modulus 750,000 psf. Because of right-of-way constraints the embankment edges are retained by MSE walls; embankment width 60 ft; MSE reinforcement length 15 ft (Figure 6-23). Paving occurs 60 days after embankment construction, and the maximum post-pavement settlement is 2.5 inches. Column design is not included, and the bearing layer is very stiff, so settlement into or of the bearing layer is not considered (pp. 6-56 to 6-57).
key_points: H = 20.5 ft; soft clay 20 ft thick, Su = 250 psf; groundwater 3 ft below grade.
Fill 115 pcf, phi' 30 deg, Ka 0.33; bridging layer 130 pcf, phi' 40 deg.
Embankment 60 ft wide with MSE walls (15 ft reinforcement).
Maximum post-pavement settlement 2.5 in.; paving 60 days after construction.
figures: Figure 6-23: General cross-section.
sections.applicability: Input data for the first CSE worked example.

sections.title: Solution
sections.summary: Twelve-step solution: 7 ft triangular spacing of 3 ft columns (ratio 17%), Qr = 113 kips, VCC columns, Hcrit 7.64 ft < 20.5 ft, settlement 2.9 in. without a bridging layer and 2.5 in. with a reinforced 3 ft layer, PLat 9,665 lb/ft vs. Rls 3,750 lb/ft, two lateral geosynthetic layers of 4,833 lb/ft.
sections.body: Step 1: use an area replacement ratio of 3.5 to 10% and clear span below H/1.5 = 13.7 ft but no more than 10 ft; a conservative 7 ft triangular spacing with 3 ft column top diameter is chosen: column area 7.07 ft2, s' = [(7^2 + 2*7^2)^(1/2)/3] - 3/2 = 2.54 ft, Aunitcell = 7(7^2 - 7^2/4)^(1/2) = 42.43 ft2, ratio 7.07/42.43 = 17% (Figure 6-24). Step 2: De = 1.05*7 = 7.35 ft; with an assumed 3 ft bridging layer (130 pcf), Qr = pi(7.35/2)^2 (115*17.5 + 130*3 + 250) = 113 kips. Step 3: aggregate, cement based or driven columns fit; a 3 ft VCC is assumed. Step 4: column capacity not included. Step 5: MSE walls on both sides, so columns span the full width. Step 6: Hcritical = 1.5*(2*2.54) = 7.64 ft < 20.5 ft OK. Step 7: GeogridBridge gives 2.9 in. post-pavement settlement without a bridging layer, more than 2.5 in., so one is required (Figures 6-25, 6-26). Step 8: a 3 ft bridging layer with two biaxial geogrid layers (long-term allowable strength 1,000 lb/ft, stiffness 24,000 lb/ft) gives 2.5 in., satisfying the requirement. Step 9: columns reach the edge, so lateral extent is not an issue. Step 10: PLat = 0.33(0.5*115*20.5^2 + 250*20.5) = 9,665 lb/ft; Rls = 15*250 = 3,750 lb/ft, so lateral spreading may occur; two layers of lateral spreading geosynthetic tying the walls together each need 4,833 lb/ft long-term strength (Figures 6-27, 6-28). Step 11: biaxial bridging and uniaxial lateral reinforcement are kept separate. Step 12: global stability not analyzed, as a true CSE has very little potential for global instability; Chapter 5 gives guidance if required (pp. 6-57 to 6-64).
key_points: Area replacement ratio 17% for 7 ft triangular spacing of 3 ft columns.
Qr = 113 kips.
Hcritical = 7.64 ft < H = 20.5 ft.
Post-pavement settlement 2.9 in. without bridging layer; 2.5 in. with a 3 ft layer and two geogrids (J = 24,000 lb/ft).
PLat = 9,665 lb/ft exceeds Rls = 3,750 lb/ft; two geosynthetic layers at 4,833 lb/ft each.
equations: Eq. 6-1: Qr = pi (De/2)^2 (gamma_e H2 + gamma_bl H1 + q) = pi (7.35/2)^2 (115*17.5 + 130*3 + 250) = 113 kips; required column load in the example
Eq. 6-3: PLat = Ka (0.5 gamma H^2 + q H) = 0.33 (0.5*115*20.5^2 + 250*20.5) = 9,665 lb/ft; lateral spreading force in the example
Eq. 6-4: Rls = Ls Su = 15*250 = 3,750 lb/ft; subgrade resistance in the example

sections.title: Example Problem 2
sections.summary: Example 2 adds a 5 ft sand layer at subgrade above 20 ft of soft clay and checks only Step 7: with 7 ft triangular spacing post-pavement settlement is 0.9 in., so spacing is increased; at 7 ft 9 in. it is 2.1 in., within the 2.5 in. limit.
sections.body: Example Problem 2 is similar to Example 1, but with a 5-foot thick sand layer at subgrade over a 20-foot thick soft clay layer. Sand properties: thickness 5 ft, unit weight 125 pcf, effective friction angle 32 degrees, Poisson's ratio 0.33, at-rest earth pressure 0.5, Young's modulus 300,000 psf. Only Step 7 (whether a bridging layer is required) is analyzed, using the GeogridBridge spreadsheet (Figures 6-29 and 6-30). For a triangular column spacing of 7 feet the post-pavement settlement is 0.9 inches against the requirement of 2.5 inches or less, so the column spacing is increased to improve the economics; at a spacing of 7 feet 9 inches the post-pavement settlement is 2.1 inches (pp. 6-64 to 6-67).
key_points: Sand at subgrade: 5 ft, 125 pcf, phi' 32 deg, E = 300,000 psf.
7 ft triangular spacing: 0.9 in. post-pavement settlement.
7 ft 9 in. spacing: 2.1 in., within the 2.5 in. limit.
